title: A friction circle and limit curves: when does it slip?
summary: Acceleration demands are plotted as points in the plane of lateral against longitudinal acceleration. The limit of available friction is a circle: points inside grip, points outside slip.

media.alt: A round plot with an orange circle of radius about 10.8 and a dotted inner circle. Most teal dots are inside the circle labelled grip, and five pink crosses outside the circle are labelled slip.
media.caption: Reference render of class F4.6 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: When does it slip?
read_the_figure.axes: Horizontal: lateral acceleration a_y in m/s^2, -15 to 15. Vertical: longitudinal acceleration a_x in m/s^2, -15 to 17. Equal scale. Orange circle: |a| = mu g with mu = 1.1 (radius 10.8 m/s^2). Dotted circle: 70 percent of the limit.
look_at: How many points lie outside the circle and what does that mean?
What longitudinal acceleration is left if the lateral acceleration is 9 m/s^2?
Do inside points guarantee grip in reality?
What is the dotted inner circle for?
as_drawn: Limit: |a| = mu g = 1.1 x 9.81 = 10.8 m/s^2. 26 sample points: 21 inside (teal dots, grip) and 5 outside (pink crosses, slip).
The dotted inner circle at 0.7 of the limit (7.55 m/s^2) is drawn but not explained in the legend: a reader must guess it is a safety margin.
The points are random synthetic samples, not a measured manoeuvre. Equal axes are used, so the circle is a circle.
read_the_figure.proves: That, under the model of a constant friction coefficient and normal force, each plotted demand is within or outside the grip limit. It says nothing about stability, about how the demand was reached, or about real tyres.
if_wrong: Unequal axes: the circle becomes an ellipse and the limit looks anisotropic.
A limit curve with no statement of the coefficient: the plot cannot be reproduced.
Points drawn without distinguishing inside from outside: the key message is lost.

terms.meaning: The set of combined accelerations the tyre can provide, a circle of radius mu g.
The ratio of the largest friction force to the normal force.
Sideways (cornering) and forward or backward (accelerating, braking) components.
The boundary beyond which the model says slip occurs.
Using grip for braking and cornering at once: they share the same budget.
The force pressing the surface against the tyre, here mg on level ground.

remember: The friction budget is a circle: sqrt(a_x^2 + a_y^2) <= mu g.
Cornering uses up braking capacity: they share one circle.
Equal axes; label the limit with mu and its radius.
Inside the circle means friction suffices, not that the vehicle is stable.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position carries the two acceleration components. The orange circle is a line mark for the limit; teal dots and pink crosses are point marks with two shapes and colours for grip and slip, so the classification survives colour blindness. The dotted ring is a reference at 70 percent.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Friction is limited by mu N in any direction along the surface, so the largest horizontal force is the same in every direction: a circle. Splitting acceleration into lateral and longitudinal parts then gives a picture of a budget: whatever you spend on cornering is unavailable for braking. A point's distance from the centre is the demand and the circle's radius is the supply.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Real tyres give an ellipse, not a circle, and the radius changes with load and speed. A constant mu and N is a model. Inside the circle does not mean safe: the demand might have been reached through a transient that exceeds the limit. Random synthetic points look like data but are not. And an unexplained inner ring invites a wrong interpretation.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The limit curve is the whole figure: without it the points are scatter. Equal axes keep the circle round. Giving mu makes the limit a number the reader can check. This render marks the limit and the grip and slip points but leaves the inner ring unexplained.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A g-g diagram with the colour of each point set by speed or time shows how a real manoeuvre uses the budget. A friction ellipse with different mu in x and y fits real tyres. A time plot of the demand against the limit shows margin. For static cases a friction cone diagram (F4.1) is the same idea in force space.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw a measured manoeuvre as a path joining the points in time order, colour it by time, and replace the circle with an ellipse using mu_x = 1.2 and mu_y = 1.0.

steps.title: The friction limit
steps.note: The same limit applies to the vector sum, which is why it is a circle. A point on it is on the verge of slipping.

steps.title: Trading cornering for braking
steps.note: At a_y = 9 m/s^2: a_x max = 5.95 m/s^2, only 55 percent of the straight-line value. At 70 percent of the lateral limit (7.55) the remaining braking capacity is 0.714 x 10.79 = 7.71 m/s^2.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure: (1) how many points slip? (2) What is the braking capacity while cornering at 9 m/s^2? (3) What is the radius of the limit circle?

solution.text: Five pink crosses lie outside the orange circle.
The remaining longitudinal capacity is the other side of a right triangle with hypotenuse 10.79 and one side 9.
mu g = 1.1 x 9.81, about 10.8 m/s^2 (the circle crosses the axes near 10.8).

worked.answer: Five of 26 demands exceed the limit; at 9 m/s^2 lateral only 5.95 m/s^2 of braking remains; the radius is 10.8 m/s^2.

checks.q: Why is the limit a circle?
checks.hint: Friction is the same in all directions.
checks.answer: The maximum friction force mu N is the same in every direction on the surface, so the allowed vector set is a disc.

checks.q: mu = 0.8. What is the maximum combined acceleration?
A point at (a_x, a_y) = (6, 9). Does it grip when mu g = 10.79?
checks.answer: sqrt(36 + 81) = 10.82, just beyond the limit of 10.79: slip is marginal, so the point is effectively on the circle.
